Heating renovation in Vancouver—the city with Canada's most diverse housing stock and one of its coldest winter climates, requiring reliable heating from October through April—ranges in cost from $3,000 for a basic baseboard heater replacement to over $18,000 for a complete ducted heat pump system with new ductwork distribution. For a typical Vancouver single-family home, a complete heating system replacement in 2026 typically costs $7,000 to $16,000, driven by BC's increasingly strict energy efficiency requirements under BC Building Code Part 6 (HVAC), the City of Vancouver's zoning rules governing equipment placement, and FortisBC's rebate requirements for gas-fired equipment. Reno Stars has been completing heating renovation projects across Vancouver, Burnaby, Richmond, and the North Shore since 2015, and Vancouver homeowners should understand that any gas-fired heating equipment requires a FortisBC gas permit and must be installed by a registered gas contractor, while electric heating systems fall under Technical Safety BC electrical oversight and qualify for BC Hydro rebates in 2026.

Vancouver Heating Regulations: What Requires a Permit

Heating renovation in Vancouver is governed by multiple overlapping regulatory frameworks:

  • BC Building Code Part 6 (HVAC) sets minimum efficiency standards for new heating equipment in Vancouver's climate zone. As of 2022, the BC Building Code requires a minimum AFUE 95% for new gas furnaces and a minimum HSPF 7.2 for air-source heat pumps in Vancouver.
  • Technical Safety BC oversees all heating equipment installation in BC, including gas fitting (furnaces, boilers, gas fireplaces) and electrical work (electric furnaces, baseboard heaters, heat pumps). All heating contractors in Vancouver must hold appropriate Technical Safety BC certifications.
  • FortisBC regulates gas-fired heating equipment and requires a gas permit for any new gas connection, furnace or boiler replacement, or gas line extension in Vancouver. FortisBC gas permits must be obtained by a registered FortisBC gas contractor—a homeowner cannot legally obtain this permit themselves.
  • The City of Vancouver's zoning bylaw (Zoning and Development By-law) governs the placement of outdoor heating equipment including heat pump outdoor units, condensing units, and gas meter locations. Equipment must meet setback requirements from property lines and cannot exceed noise level thresholds at the property boundary.
  • Vancouver's Vancouver Building Bylaw sets additional requirements for heating system replacements, including proper sizing calculations, distribution system design, and combustion air requirements for gas-fired equipment.
  • For strata properties in Vancouver, the Strata Property Act requires that any heating work affecting common property receive strata council approval before work begins, and many Vancouver strata buildings have specific bylaws governing exterior HVAC and heating equipment.
  • BC Hydro offers rebates for electric heating upgrades including heat pumps and electric furnaces in the Vancouver service area in 2026, ranging from $500 to $4,000 depending on equipment type and eligibility.
  • FortisBC offers rebates for gas-fired heating equipment in Vancouver, including up to $1,000 for qualifying high-efficiency furnace replacements and combination boiler systems in 2026.

Heating System Options for Vancouver Homes

Vancouver homes use a range of heating system types, each with different costs, efficiency ratings, and regulatory requirements:

  • Forced-air gas furnace (most common in Vancouver single-family homes): heats air and distributes through ductwork; most Vancouver homes built after 1970 use this system type
  • Gravity-fed gas furnace (older Vancouver homes, particularly pre-1970): uses natural convection rather than a blower; being phased out but still found in Vancouver's older housing stock in Strathcona, Mount Pleasant, and Hastings-Sunrise
  • Hot water (hydronic) radiator heating: uses a boiler to heat water distributed through radiators or baseboard convectors; common in Vancouver's 1920s–1950s character homes in Shaughnessy, Kerrisdale, and Point Grey
  • Ductless mini-split heat pump: electric-powered without ductwork; ideal for Vancouver homes without existing ducts, including many character homes and laneway houses
  • Ducted heat pump: electric-powered central heating and cooling; growing in popularity in Vancouver following FortisBC and BC Hydro rebate increases in 2024–2026
  • Electric baseboard heaters: individual room-by-room heating; common in Vancouver condos and apartments; relatively inexpensive to install but higher operating costs
  • Radiant floor heating (hydronic or electric): heats from the floor up; often installed in Vancouver bathroom and kitchen renovations as a supplemental heating source
  • Combination (tankless) boiler: provides both space heating and hot water from a single gas-fired unit; increasingly popular in Vancouver renovations for its efficiency and space savings

Gas Furnace and Boiler Costs

  • High-efficiency gas furnace (AFUE 95%+, new installation): $4,000–$9,000 for equipment, $1,500–$3,500 for installation, total $5,500–$12,500
  • Gas furnace replacement (existing location, same configuration): $3,000–$7,000 for equipment, $1,000–$2,500 for installation, total $4,000–$9,500
  • Gravity-fed gas furnace replacement (older Vancouver homes): $4,500–$10,000 for equipment, $2,000–$4,500 for installation, total $6,500–$14,500 (often requires ductwork modification)
  • High-efficiency gas boiler (hot water radiant): $5,000–$12,000 for equipment, $2,000–$5,000 for installation, total $7,000–$17,000
  • Combination (tankless) boiler: $5,500–$13,000 for equipment, $2,000–$5,000 for installation, total $7,500–$18,000
  • Gas fireplace insert (direct-vent, existing fireplace): $2,000–$5,000 for equipment, $500–$1,500 for installation, total $2,500–$6,500

Heat Pump and Electric Heating Costs

  • Ductless mini-split heat pump (single zone): $2,500–$7,000 for equipment, $1,500–$3,000 for installation, total $4,000–$10,000
  • Ductless mini-split heat pump (multi-zone, up to 5 rooms): $6,000–$14,000 for equipment, $2,000–$5,000 for installation, total $8,000–$19,000
  • Ducted heat pump system (replacing existing ducts): $8,000–$18,000 for equipment, $3,000–$6,000 for ductwork modification, total $11,000–$24,000
  • Electric furnace replacement: $1,500–$4,000 for equipment, $1,000–$2,500 for installation, total $2,500–$6,500
  • Electric baseboard heater replacement (per unit, including installation): $300–$800 per heater
  • Radiant floor heating (electric mat system, per square foot): $15–$30 per square foot for equipment and installation
  • Hydronic radiant floor heating (boiler-fed, per square foot): $25–$60 per square foot for equipment and installation

Permits and Associated Costs

  • FortisBC gas permit (furnace/boiler work): $100–$250 — must be obtained by registered FortisBC gas contractor
  • Technical Safety BC electrical permit (heat pump, electric heating): $100–$200
  • City of Vancouver building permit for stand-alone heating work: $150–$500
  • Heating load calculation (required for new ducted systems): $200–$500
  • Ductwork modification or extension: $2,000–$8,000 depending on scope
  • Smart thermostat (Nest, ecobee, etc.): $200–$500 + $50–$150 installation
  • Annual heating system maintenance contract (Vancouver): $150–$400 per year

Frequently Asked Questions About Heating Renovation in Vancouver

Do I need a permit to replace my furnace in Vancouver?

Yes, replacing a gas furnace in Vancouver requires both a FortisBC gas permit and typically a City of Vancouver building permit. The FortisBC gas permit must be obtained by a registered gas contractor before any work begins—a homeowner cannot legally obtain this permit themselves. The permit covers the gas connection and ensures the installation meets BC's Gas Safety Regulation and BC Building Code Part 6. A Vancouver building permit is also required when the work involves modifying the existing flue or chimney, adding or relocating a gas line, or installing a furnace in a new location. Simple like-for-like furnace replacements in the same location with the same configuration may not require a full building permit but still require the FortisBC gas permit. Your registered gas contractor will advise on the specific permit requirements for your Vancouver home.

What heating rebates are available for Vancouver homeowners in 2026?

Vancouver homeowners can access heating renovation rebates from multiple sources in 2026. FortisBC offers up to $1,000 for qualifying high-efficiency gas furnace replacements and combination boiler systems. BC Hydro offers $500–$4,000 for qualifying heat pump installations, including both ductless mini-splits and ducted heat pump systems. The federal Canada Greener Homes Grant provides up to $5,000 for eligible heat pump installations, stackable with provincial rebates. These rebates are stackable for qualifying households—Reno Stars assists Vancouver homeowners with all rebate applications as part of our standard heating renovation estimate process. Applications must generally be submitted before work begins—do not sign a contract with a heating contractor before confirming your rebate eligibility, as some programs require pre-approval.

How long does a heating renovation take in Vancouver?

A typical heating renovation in Vancouver—a like-for-like gas furnace replacement—takes 1 to 3 business days for the installation work itself. However, the full project timeline must account for: permit acquisition (FortisBC gas permits typically 3–7 business days; Vancouver building permits for heating work 5–15 business days if required), equipment ordering and delivery (1–4 weeks for non-stock items), and any required inspections by Technical Safety BC and the City of Vancouver (scheduled within 1–3 business days of the contractor's request). For a complete ducted heat pump system replacement in a Vancouver home, the full project timeline is typically 4 to 8 weeks from signed contract to final inspection. For a gravity-fed furnace replacement in an older Vancouver character home that requires ductwork modification, plan for an additional 1–2 weeks. 温哥华的供暖装修——加拿大最多样化住房库存和最寒冷冬季气候的城市之一，10月至4月需要可靠供暖——费用从基本踢脚板 heater更换的$3,000到全管道热泵系统（含新管道分配系统）的$18,000以上不等。对于典型的温哥华独立屋，2026年完整供暖系统更换费用通常为$7,000至$16,000，驱动因素包括BC省在BC建筑规范第6部分（暖通空调）下越来越严格的能效要求、温哥华市规范设备摆放位置的区划规则，以及FortisBC对燃气设备的补贴要求。聚星装修自2015年以来一直在温哥华、本拿比、列治文及北岸完成供暖装修项目，而温哥华业主应了解任何燃气供暖设备都需要FortisBC煤气许可证，必须由注册煤气承包商安装，而电动供暖系统则归Technical Safety BC电气监督管辖，并有资格在2026年获得BC Hydro补贴。

温哥华供暖法规：需要许可证的情况

温哥华的供暖装修受多个重叠监管框架管辖：

  • BC建筑规范第6部分（暖通空调）为温哥华气候区新供暖设备设定最低效率标准。自2022年起，BC建筑规范要求新燃气炉最低AFUE 95%，空气源热泵最低HSPF 7.2。
  • Technical Safety BC监管BC省所有供暖设备安装，包括煤气管道工程（炉子、锅炉、燃气壁炉）和电气工程（电炉、踢脚板 heater、热泵）。温哥华所有供暖承包商必须持有适当的Technical Safety BC认证。
  • FortisBC监管燃气供暖设备，需要对温哥华任何新燃气连接、炉子或锅炉更换或燃气管道延伸办理煤气许可证。FortisBC煤气许可证必须由注册的FortisBC煤气承包商办理——业主自己无法合法办理此许可证。
  • 温哥华市的区划附例（《区划和发展附例》）管辖户外供暖设备（包括热泵室外机、冷凝机组和燃气表位置）的摆放位置。设备必须满足与物业线的退让要求，且在物业边界不得超过噪音水平阈值。
  • 温哥华建筑附例为供暖系统更换设定了额外要求，包括适当的 sizing 计算、分配系统设计以及燃气设备的燃烧空气要求。
  • 对于温哥华的共有产权物业，根据《共有产权物业法》，任何影响公共财产的供暖工程在工作开始前需要共有产权委员会批准，许多温哥华共有产权建筑有管理户外暖通空调和供暖设备的专门附例。
  • BC Hydro在2026年为温哥华服务区的电动供暖升级（包括热泵和电炉）提供$500至$4,000不等的补贴，取决于设备类型和资格。
  • FortisBC为温哥华的燃气供暖设备提供补贴，包括2026年符合资格的高效炉子更换和组合锅炉系统最高$1,000。

温哥华房屋使用多种供暖系统类型，每种有不同的费用、效率等级和监管要求：

  • 重力式燃气炉（温哥华较老房屋，特别是1970年前）：使用自然对流而非鼓风机；在Strathcona、Mount Pleasant和Hastings-Sunrise的温哥华老旧住房库存中仍有存在，但正在被淘汰
  • 热水（液压）散热器供暖：使用锅炉加热分配到散热器或踢脚板 convective heaters的水；在Shaughnessy、Kerrisdale和Point Grey的1920年代至1950年代特色房屋中常见
  • 管道less分体式热泵：无管道电动供暖；适合没有现有管道的温哥华房屋，包括许多特色住宅和巷道房屋
  • 管道热泵：电动中央供暖和制冷；在2024至2026年FortisBC和BC Hydro补贴增加后，在温哥华越来越受欢迎
  • 电动踢脚板 heater：按房间一对一供暖；常见于温哥华公寓和共管公寓；安装相对便宜但运营成本较高
  • 辐射地板供暖（液压或电动）：从地板向上加热；通常作为补充供暖源安装在温哥华浴室和厨房装修中
  • 组合（即热式）锅炉：从单一燃气设备提供空间供暖和热水；因效率和节省空间而在温哥华装修中越来越受欢迎

关于温哥华供暖装修的常见问题

在温哥华更换炉子需要许可证吗？
